self-reported adherence measures have moderate agreement and that the visual analog scale captures more potentially non-adherent people.

The visual analog scale (measuring adherence over the past month) captured the greatest number and most severe non-adherent individuals, and depression was strongly associated with non-adherence irrespective of the measure of adherence used.

self-reported adherence was high, depression was associated with lower self-reported adherence, but HIV-related stigma was not associated with self-reported adherence, and that the VAS captured the largest number of potentially nonadherent individuals.

the measurement of adherence to antireviroviral therapy (ARV), a critical factor in the treatment of HIV/AIDS.
the development of a new measure of antiretrovival therapy adherence that is suitable for use in non-clinicial settings in India.
the development, validation, and use of measures of adherence, depression, and HIV-related stigma in non-clinically based HIV-infected populations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
adherence is very high, and the best way to measure it is to ask people how many days they missed their medications, and that depression is the strongest predictor of poor adherence.

the VAS may be a useful tool to measure adherence in non-clinics, and the association between adherence and depression is strong enough to warrant further research into the potential of a joint approach to address both issues in PLHA.

The main takeaway from our work is that
adherence measures may be useful for understanding adherence in non-clinically based populations.

the VAS is a simple measure that can be used to identify individuals in need of adherence counseling, and that depression is a strong and independent predictor of poorer adherence in non-clinician settings.
there is no one adherence measure that is optimal for identifying PLHA with poor adherence, and the measure used should be tailored to the context and purpose of assessment.
